nameStory: The ruddy duck gets its name from the rich, rusty-red plumage that males sport during breeding season, giving them a distinctly 'ruddy' appearance. These chunky little ducks have earned the nickname 'butterball' due to their short, stout build that makes them look somewhat plump and makes walking on land quite awkward for them.
description: Ruddy ducks are small, compact waterfowl known for their distinctive stiff tails that they often hold upright like a periscope. Males in breeding plumage display brilliant reddish-brown bodies with bright blue bills, while females and non-breeding males are more subdued in brown tones. They're built more like floating tennis balls than typical ducks, with their round bodies sitting low in the water. These diving ducks are excellent swimmers but struggle on land due to their legs being positioned far back on their bodies.

idTips.label: Stiff, upright tail
idTips.description: The tail feathers are notably rigid and often held straight up at a 45-degree angle, looking like a small rudder sticking out of the water

idTips.label: Compact, round body
idTips.description: Sits very low in the water with a distinctly round, almost ball-like silhouette that looks different from other ducks

idTips.label: Male breeding colors
idTips.description: Bright rusty-red body with a striking powder-blue bill that looks almost artificial in its intensity

idTips.label: Female and winter plumage
idTips.description: Mottled brown and gray coloring with a distinctive dark line running horizontally across the pale cheek

idTips.label: Swimming behavior
idTips.description: Often disappears completely underwater when diving, popping up unexpectedly in a different spot like a feathered submarine

habitat: Look for ruddy ducks in shallow, marshy ponds, quiet lake coves, and wetlands with plenty of emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges. They prefer areas with muddy bottoms rich in aquatic invertebrates and are often found in the same spots as red-winged blackbirds and great blue herons. During migration and winter, they may appear in larger, more open bodies of water including coastal ponds and protected bays.

seasonality.spring: Males begin showing their brilliant rusty breeding plumage and bright blue bills as they arrive at nesting areas, often engaging in elaborate courtship displays with tail fanning and head bobbing.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season when males are at their most colorful and females may be seen with broods of ducklings following behind in marshy areas.
seasonality.fall: Males molt into duller brown winter plumage, making them harder to distinguish from females as they gather in flocks for migration.
seasonality.winter: Present in more open water areas in subdued brown plumage, often in mixed flocks with other diving ducks, though some individuals may remain year-round in ice-free areas.

funFact: Ruddy ducks are such poor walkers that they essentially can't move on land at all - their legs are positioned so far back on their bodies that they have to push themselves along on their bellies like feathered seals, making them one of the most water-dependent ducks in North America.
confusionNotes: In winter plumage, ruddy ducks might be confused with female ring-necked ducks or lesser scaup, but the ruddy's distinctive stiff tail held upright and extremely compact, round body shape are dead giveaways. Remember: if it looks like a floating tennis ball with a periscope tail, it's a ruddy duck.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being native to the Americas, ruddy ducks have become a controversial invasive species in Europe after being introduced to the UK in the 1940s, where they've caused ecological problems by hybridizing with endangered native white-headed ducks in Spain.
compareHints: Ruddy ducks are the only stiff-tailed ducks regularly found in New England, making them unique among our waterfowl for their upright tail posture. While other diving ducks like ring-necked ducks and lesser scaup share their diving behavior, none have the ruddy's distinctive round body shape, stiff tail, or the male's brilliant blue bill during breeding season.
